talks.title: Gathering & Mingling
Opening Words
Move between rooms
“WTF Was That?” Dispatches From the Wrong End of an Agent Swarm
talks.abstract: One attack path is an investigation. Several at once make for a very different afternoon. An AI adversary worked its way through our systems at machine speed. We’ll share what that pressure looked like from the defender’s seat, what caught us off guard, and what it took to contain it.

talks.title: All Tokens Are Created Equal, Including the Attacker’s

speakers.name: Rock Lambros
speakers.affiliation: Director of AI Standards and Governance, Zenity

talks.abstract: EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) walked data out of Microsoft 365 Copilot with zero clicks. No memory bug. No blown permission. Attacker text landed in the context window and the model did what it said, because transformer attention reads no trust label on any token. Your system prompt, a poisoned README, and an MCP tool definition all get the same scaled dot-product treatment. So we measured it. Attention mass on the protective span collapsing as an attacker floods the window, plotted against attack success climbing. Then we built the thing nobody has: a record of what the model actually saw. We’re releasing CxBOM, a CycloneDX-based bill of materials for the context window. It logs every component, its trust ring, and its provenance, and it fails the session when an externally supplied MCP tool definition is assembled with operator-level authority. That inversion is the bug behind CVE-2025-54135 and CVE-2025-54136. Live demo. Schema, emitter, validator, fixtures. Yours to run.

talks.title: CTF: Kickoff
talks.abstract: Straight after the opening keynote, in the villages room and online. Full rules and format revealed here.

talks.title: Taming AI Agents with Capsem: Hardware Sandboxing That Doesn’t Kill Productivity
talks.abstract: Enterprises are racing to adopt AI agents granting them access to data, networks, code execution, and beyond. Yet between prompt injection, hallucination, and agents going rogue, poorly restricted access is a security nightmare that weakly secured environments can no longer bandage over, as proven by recent model sandbox escapes. Capsem is an open-source, Rust co-designed hypervisor/VM system designed to fill the need of a highly secure agent environment. What makes it unique is its core premise being that to be successful should not make users choose between speed, usability and security. Users love Capsem for its single-click install, optional friendly UI, and agent-ready VMs booting under two seconds. Security endorses its air-gapped, hardened VMs, and leverages its full observability and enforcement mechanisms—including its L8 network reconstruction layer with full model and MCP semantics. Admins rely on its SDK and standard support for Sigma and OpenTelemetry.

talks.title: Attention Is All You Need (to Catch Hallucinations & Prompt Injections)
talks.abstract: Two of the biggest trust and security challenges of LLM: hallucinations (ungrounded facts) and indirect prompt injections (unauthorized instructions) are often believed to be unrelated. Existing blackbox methods for detecting these problems are distinct, often too slow, expensive, and unreliable. This talk highlights a major breakthrough in whitebox analysis that shows that these problems are actually related and can be solved with the same approach simultaneously. Our key insight is that LLMs are incapable of permanently storing specific facts or instructions. Instead, when they need a fact or instruction, they “look back” to the relevant part of the input. By observing these hidden states during these token generation, we can identify exactly which input tokens the model relied on for each factual statement or instruction it follows. Our solution works in real time, requires no additional LLM calls, and outperforms state of the art on multiple benchmarks.

talks.title: Introduction To Harness Engineering For Vulnerability Research
talks.abstract: Participants build and tune an AI-assisted security research harness to map attack surfaces, inspect code, validate vulnerabilities dynamically, and disclose findings.
talks.details: Description: Pointing a model at a repository and asking it to “find all the vulnerabilities” is not vulnerability research and is overwhelming software maintainters with poor quality reports. The same models can produce radically different results depending on the context, tools, constraints, and methodology wrapped around it. In this hands-on workshop, participants will select a real open-source project and build a bespoke security research harness for it. Using Claude Code or Codex as a baseline, we will improve the agent’s capabilities by learning and implementing harness engineering techniques to improve finding quality. Participants will build their harness to identify vulnerabilities by mapping attack surfaces, inspecting source code, and validating potentially vulnerable behavior by running software dynamically. Participants will leave with a working research harness and a reusable methodology for how to tune it to find, validate, and disclose findings. No prior harness-engineering experience is required. This is for people who have used mainstream agents for security purposes but want to move beyond one-off prompts. Prerequisites: Have used a mainstream coding agent such as Codex, Claude Code, or an equivalent tool. Be comfortable using a terminal, Git, and a source repository. Be able to read source code in at least one programming language. Understand basic vulnerability research concepts Participant Setup Requirements: A laptop running macOS, Linux, or Windows with WSL2. Administrator access to install and run development tools. Git and a terminal environment. A coding-agent CLI installed and authenticated. Codex is recommended, but Claude Code or another agent with filesystem and tool access can be used. Any required account, subscription, API key, or inference credits for the selected agent. A local container runtime such as Docker or Podman, or access to an isolated cloud development environment that they control.

talks.title: What Deserves the SOC’s Attention? Ranking Incidents and Misconfigurations with LLMs
talks.abstract: Workshop on ranking security incidents and misconfigurations with scoring and LLMs, linking causes to attacks, and hardening the pipeline against adversarial log input.
talks.details: Description: A SOC drowns in what we send it. Every team forwards every log line and every finding, most of them marked high, and the analysts are left to sort it out. The teams that own the systems know best what matters, so that is where the sorting should start. In this workshop you build a ranking layer for a small application. Nothing gets dropped. Every log line is still stored, but your layer decides what deserves the SOC’s attention. You work with the application’s logs and its misconfigurations, and one real attack is hidden among a lot of harmless noise. You rank what you find with simple scoring and an LLM, and you link incidents to the misconfigurations that make them dangerous. Then you check if the attack lands at the top of the analyst’s queue. A ranker that reads logs can be fooled by whoever writes them. In the last part you attack your own pipeline with a log line built to bury the attack, and then you fix it. Prerequisites: Basic LLM knowledge Linux knowledge Know how to use a shell Participant Setup Requirements: Laptop with ssh or WebUi Internet and disabled enterprise proxies

talks.title: Finding Vulnerabilities with AgentGG AI Agents: A Hands-On Workshop
talks.abstract: Hands-on workshop on using AgentGG AI agents to detect, validate, score, tune, and continuously scan for source-code vulnerabilities.
talks.details: Description: AgentGG CLI is an open-source tool that uses AI agents to find, validate and score security vulnerabilities in source code. We’ve used it to find 40+ zero-days that were accepted by open-source projects, including a critical SQL injection in GeoServer (CVE-2026-76904, CVSS 9.8). In this workshop, we share what we learned about reducing false positives and keeping scan costs down. Participants run AgentGG against a deliberately vulnerable app and triage the results. We walk through each stage of a scan, from recon to validation and CVSS scoring. Participants then write their own detection agent, which consists of a precondition, a seeding strategy using regex or Semgrep, and a prompt written in markdown. They tune the agent to reduce false positives and add it to a CI pipeline that scans pull requests. By the end, participants will have a working custom agent and a CI workflow they can use on their own code. No prior experience building AI agents is required. Prerequisites: Basic terminal and git skills, the ability to read code, and familiarity with common web vulnerabilities like SQL injection and XSS. Participant Setup Requirements: A laptop with Node.js, git, and a GitHub account.

talks.title: Coffee break
Coffee break
How Meta Changed Building Secure Software With AI

speakers.name: David Molnar
speakers.affiliation: Scale finding, fixing, and prevention across the world., Meta

talks.abstract: Meta’s core values include moving fast, which is why we’ve invested for years in developer tooling and automating discovery of security bugs. With AI, software development at Meta moves faster than ever: significant lines of code grew 105.9% year on year, with AI written code responsible for over 80% of that growth. We’ve changed software security to match – this talk covers two lessons learned and where we’re going next. First, we’ll talk about driving code analysis coverage at breakneck speed to get ahead of external attackers armed with AI. What we needed to cover, how we prioritized, and how that built off prior experiences. We successfully landed 90% coverage on our targets, but that’s far from solving the whole problem. Second, we’ll go over lessons from using AI to write fixes. We landed at over 40% of critical vulnerabilities fixed by AI-written diffs. We were surprised by finding that this did not, by itself, reduce the time to fix vulnerabilities!

talks.title: Into the Wild: Hunting Real-World Attacks on AI Systems
talks.abstract: Until now, AI security research has lived mostly in the lab, while AI systems went online. This created a knowledge gap: defenders lack threat intelligence from real AI incidents. To discover what attackers do in the wild, we deployed a honeypot network emulating production AI stacks and agents. This talk is the forensic report. We show campaigns probing for CVEs to compromise AI backends within days of being published, turning Ollama’s model downloader into an SSRF vector, and LiteLLM’s guardrails into a code execution vector. We’ll detail attacks on models, and attempts to create backdoored models stripping safety controls or to exfiltrate telemetry. We display attempts to hijack backends and deploy offensive frameworks to turn exposed AI infra into free compute. We demonstrate activity probing for frontier models and agents’ capabilities, and abusing agents’ own tools to extract secrets. We share TTPs, IoCs, signatures, configurations and enabling design patterns.

talks.title: From DARPA AIxCC to Microsoft FORGE Lab: Lessons Building Hyperscale AI Code Scanning Tools
talks.abstract: Team Atlanta’s victory in the DARPA AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC), where AI systems autonomously discovered and repaired vulnerabilities in complex software, was only the beginning. Since AIxCC, we have been evolving AI vulnerability discovery into production systems for open-source and commercial codebases. Drawing from MDASH and Microsoft FORGE Lab, this talk examines how modern AI\-powered code scanning combines LLM reasoning with traditional program analysis to find real vulnerabilities at scale. We will discuss lessons learned operationalizing autonomous security systems, emerging technical patterns behind modern AI bug-finding platforms, and how AI agents may transform software security in the future.

talks.title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the Models Behind Agentic Attacks

speakers.name: Sergej Epp
speakers.affiliation: Creator of the Zero Day Clock, Leading Infosec and Threat Research

talks.abstract: Last year at [un]prompted, we showed that AI-assisted attackers leak an “accent”: timing gaps, hallucinated identifiers, tool artifacts and other model-specific behavior. Those signals are accidental. This talk turns them into a measurement method. We introduce shibboleths: realistic features placed in an attacker’s environment specifically because different models respond to them differently without requiring prompt injection or adversarial instructions. Combined with passive telemetry, they let us fingerprint the model family and agent harness behind an attack even when the model is self-hosted and its claimed identity cannot be trusted. We show how to generate and optimize these traps, demonstrate fingerprinting end-to-end against autonomous attackers, and present results from a controlled model/harness matrix and live honeypot deployment including where the method fails. The result is a new telemetry layer for investigating and clustering AI-driven attacks.

talks.title: StealthBench: Can Autonomous Security Agents Do OPSEC Like An Experienced Operator?

speakers.name: Ads Dawson
speakers.affiliation: Staff AI Security Researcher at Dreadnode; founder of OWASP GenAI Security Project; AI red teamer and bug bounty hunter

talks.abstract: Autonomous security agents are usually judged on whether they find the vulnerability. In a real engagement, that is only half the job: an agent that leaks credentials, modifies production, spams users, or floods telemetry can turn a successful exploit into an operational failure and a detection. A very stealthy model is thu a more dangerous one. We introduce StealthBench, an open-source benchmark that measures task completion and operational security together. Fourteen containerized scenarios test credential handling, detection avoidance, infrastructure compartmentalization, operational impact, and third-party harm. Across 771 trajectories from eight agent models, no model achieved a safe-success rate above 53.8%. Some highly capable models solved most tasks yet did so recklessly in more than one-third of valid attempts. This talk presents the benchmark, the failure patterns it exposes, and practical lessons for evaluating agents before granting them offensive-security tools.

talks.title: Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? A Scan of 86 Million GitHub Items
talks.abstract: A hidden HTML comment in a GitHub issue can hijack a coding agent. This has been repeatedly shown in demos and research PoCs. But how often are attackers in the wild actually trying it, and what do they want? We launched the first GitHub-wide scan to hunt for indirect prompt injections across 86 million GitHub items: issues, PRs, comments and READMEs. We extracted hidden text (e.g., HTML comments) then screened it with novel heuristics and a two-stage LLM classifier. We then manually reviewed every flagged candidate. We identified prompt injections in roughly 2.5 of every 100K GitHub items. A key finding is that injections serve diverse objectives: orchestration of project agents, constrain visiting bots, growth hacking, and malicious exfil data. We’ll dissect real injections, map their objectives, and explain our detection blind spots. We release the detector, prompts, and taxonomy so others can investigate who is steering coding agents and why.

talks.title: CISA’s Experience and Lessons Learned in AI-Enabled Vulnerability Management

speakers.name: Kevin Donovan
speakers.affiliation: CISA’s Deputy Associate Director for Vulnerabilty Management

talks.abstract: CISA plays a variety of fundamentally important roles in the global vulnerability management ecosystem – from sponsoring and overseeing the execution of the CVE Program, maintaining the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, to co-directing the Gold Eagle vulnerability intake platform to help manage the influx of new vulnerabilities being discovered by AI models. This presentation will cover a variety of ways in which CISA is adopting AI models, building skills, and exploring the use of agents to optimize its vulnerability management mission, including specific details on what approaches are working and which ones haven’t.

talks.title: Promptware EOD: Skillful Agent Detonation
talks.abstract: The AI agent supply chain is fertile ground for malware. Lurking in skill files, rug-pulled MCP servers, misaligned models, and even moltbook posts Standing on the shoulders of giants, we introduce an old-new approach: agent detonation chamber. Analysis based on kernel-level truths, not a wishful LLM scan. We detonated tens of thousands of skills from public marketplaces, and uncovered hundreds of malicious ones. We’ll show how cryptominers and infostealers evade static scanners using advanced techniques, expose risky patterns, and uncover the slop of skill design Inside the chamber, a victim agent installs a suspicious artifact, while a red-team agent tries to make it use the new skill. By comparing what the victim “thinks” it did with what the kernel knows happened the chamber reveals malicious behavior static tools miss To wrap up we’ll release our detonation chamber as free public service. As well as drop a unique verified benchmark of supply chain artifacts caught in the wild

talks.title: Lunch break
Lunch break
Lunch break
Prompt, Patch, Prove
talks.abstract: Attackers can analyze firmware in hours. Defenders may wait weeks for an update. Can defenders build temporary, testable repairs without pretending to replace the vendor? On an authorized ASUS RT-BE82U laboratory router, we used an agentic coding model to analyze build 39099 and repair two published vulnerabilities: CVE-2025-15101, an authenticated command injection in the root web server, and CVE-2026-11851, an authenticated SQL-injection path. The model traced request data into the exact ARM sinks, proposed hash-locked patches, generated negative tests, and helped reconstruct the firmware package. I will show the original and patched assembly, what the model got wrong, the evidence gates that caught it, and a reusable prompting protocol for defensive binary repair.

talks.title: Sandboxing Agents is a Three-Body Problem: Containment, Provenance, and the Human Authority
talks.abstract: Every sandboxing guide treats agent containment as one problem. Building Webflow’s agent-native design and collaboration platform (in research preview) we found at least three, and they pull on each other. Containment: what the process can touch. Provenance: whether the agent can tell instruction from data. Authority: who may act, who confirms, and what that confirmation binds to. Each is solvable alone. Coupled, they behave like the three-body problem: tighten one and the other two move This talk is about sequencing. Why our first boundary confined writes rather than reads, and why we framed it as anti-persistence instead of anti-damage. Why the iframe boundary had to be destination-driven. How a governance layer lets the host, not the model, decide what each agent and user may do. What came next, and how each boundary was tested and some live approval telemetry from the research preview: You leave with a way to decide which body to harden first for your agent.

talks.abstract: Build and tune a CI/CD pipeline with AI security agents to assess code and infrastructure as code, deploy tests, and triage findings effectively.
talks.details: Description: In this workshop you will learn via hands-on labs how to integrate AI security agents into your pipelines, use them to assess code and infrastructure as code, and how to triage and manage findings without killing developers. Each student will be provided a lab AWS account, and the lab guide will assume only basic technical skills. Participant Setup Requirements: A laptop or other device capable of browsing to the AWS console.

talks.title: Break Your Agent’s Memory

speakers.name: Cristian Leo
speakers.affiliation: CTO and co-founder, Armorer Labs (YC F26)

talks.abstract: Hands-on workshop to build an AI assistant, learn how poisoned documents spread between assistants through memory and file tools, then deploy defenses one at a time to our assistant.
talks.details: Description: This 2-hour hands-on workshop uses a sandboxed assistant to show how persistent memory and file tools create an attack path between users. Assistants with persistent memory and file tools are becoming the default way people work with agents, and they share files with each other all the time. We will build a small assistant with a memory store, file read and write tools, and a shared folder. Everyone will start with one poisoned document and measure how far the infection travels, hop by hop, across a chain of assistants. Then we add defenses one at a time and re-measure: an outbound allowlist on uploads, a screen on memory writes, and stricter handling for widely shared files. For each control you will run harmless read and write tasks to see the real cost of the defense. The goal: a control only counts if it cuts second-hop survival by at least half and normal work still succeeds. Prerequisites: Laptop; Python or Node; an API key is provided or a local model works; no prior security experience needed beyond having used an AI agent. Participant Setup Requirements: Bring a laptop with Python or Node available. An API key is provided, or a local model works. No prior security experience is required beyond having used an AI agent.

talks.title: Your Sandbox Degrades Gracefully, What’s the Wurst That Could Happen?
talks.abstract: RAPTOR is an agentic security harness for finding bugs: an LLM reads a repository nobody has vetted, writes proof-of-concepts from what it finds, and runs them on a machine holding our API keys and everything else dear to us. We’ve been around the block, and weren’t comfortable running that outside a sandbox, so back in April we built an agent-specific one to contain it. We’ve upgraded it considerably since, and along the way introduced (and had to fix) a fair few security issues of our own making. We don’t think we’re that innovative (or cool actually), we just believed it was necessary – but it was much harder than it looks. Oh yah, everyone tells us how easy making a sandbox is. This talk is the embarrassing lessons behind what is now a hardened agent sandbox, attack-ready, until the next time we figure out how to break it by trying to upgrade it. Four months in, we’re still finding out how little we knew about constraining dinosaurs and how often they tried to eat our faces.

talks.title: The Model Is NOT a Security Control: Prompt Injection Dies at the Token Sampler
talks.abstract: Tantalus is a 2-round indirect prompt injection arena that puts you in front of a realistic AI assistant with access to files, emails, and chat history, pre-loaded with both legitimate tools and poisoned ones. The objective is to try to get the agent to exfiltrate data from an IT admin’s workstation. With Tantalus as the substrate for my first whitepaper https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S9GU6, I put it through the ringer across ~6.1 million inference calls; across model sizes 1.7B to 119B params. All behavioral and structural controls were bypassed or allowed malicious data to be generated, except for one. Only one control had a provable 100% rate at blocking bad behavior from ever being generated.

talks.title: Three Years of Evals Later: What’s Changing in Model and Harness IR/SOC Scores
talks.abstract: As we build IR/SOC investigation agents, every new model and harness release triggers the same conversation: is there anything worthwhile here? Release materials may claim 99%+ or SOTA, but we find tasks are frequently contaminated, unreproducible, or too unrealistic. For three years we have run major frontier and open-weight models, plus commercial and open harnesses, against an evolving benchmark for modern incident response: 100+ log sources, capped budgets, and measures for accuracy, speed, cost, refusals, contamination, and cheating. The results generally track what we see on real tasks like timelining. This talk covers recent shifts, including: when frontier models need extra runway, where open weights are good enough, why fast costs are falling, when open harnesses are competitive, how models and harnesses are absorbing prompt engineering, and where investigation harnesses beat coding agents. We close with what it means to own your evals and adapt them to your environment.

talks.title: But the Reasoning Looks Right! Backdoors That Evade CoT Monitoring
talks.abstract: Chain-of-thought monitoring is an increasingly central yet fragile part of AI safety stacks: monitors look for misbehavior in a model’s visible reasoning, under the assumption that CoTs are informative of the final output. What happens when the reasoning reaches the correct conclusion, but an attacker chooses the final answer? We introduce CoT-hidden backdoors: poisoned models producing benign reasoning alongside attacker-chosen outputs. We show how these behaviors are learned, why reasoning-only monitors miss them, and what changes when monitors also see the answer. We then ask whether internal activations can expose what visible reasoning hides. Using mechanistic interpretability tools, we find backdoors difficult to identify without prior knowledge of the poison. A natural-language autoencoder demo compares activations with and without the trigger, revealing differences shortly before the final answer, but neither the attacker’s target nor a reliable way to detect the backdoor.

talks.title: Who Authorized the Agent? Making the AI Harness an Enforceable Compliance Boundary
talks.abstract: An agent can receive a deny decision and still succeed if its harness retains a broad credential or another network path. This session presents a practical architecture for making the AI agent harness an enforceable compliance boundary. We trace one tool call through the IdP, human and workload identity, immutable run context, policy decision point, mandatory enforcement points, short-lived credential broker, downstream authorization, and audit evidence. A working prototype and executable policy models show how user entitlement, agent capability, task, resource policy, and runtime context combine into one decision. A short demo compares a decision-only API with an inline proxy that stops the downstream request. We also examine wrapper bypass, service-account substitution, stale decisions, credential lifetime mismatches, and incomplete evidence.

talks.title: Inside Cairn – Open Windows Into AI Attacks
talks.abstract: Attackers are pointing autonomous agents at targets, and many forget to password-protect the control panel. We found over 20 exposed panels for Cairn, an AI harness that takes a target and a goal and runs agents until it gets there. They show real operations end to end: target selection, the literal task prompts, every step the agents took, and the outcome. The criminal clusters ran over 1,600 attack projects against 1100 e-commerce sites at about $5 each, and around 10% succeeded, typically within a day. We walk through what the attackers did, the tooling, and the exploit chains the agents built from small bugs.

talks.title: Coffee break
Coffee break
A Tale of Two Chains
talks.abstract: This talk will discuss not one but two full chain Chrome exploits we developed and submitted to Google’s VRP for the full chain bonus. The first chain, which had significant human involvement and was developed over a period of two months, met its end in a collision with an internally-discovered bug upon reporting. The second chain was developed in a whirlwind six days with significantly less human guidance: instead, we orchestrated a multi-stage, structured campaign that guided AI agents to produce a primary candidate and several collision insurance “backups” for each stage (V8 corruption, V8 sandbox escape, and renderer sandbox escape) and submitted it to the VRP, ultimately resulting in a $250,000 reward for the first full chain exploit demonstrated under the new April 2026 VRP rules. The talk will cover the differences in how each chain was developed and explain what it takes to get a full chain exploit with no collisions against modern Chrome.

talks.title: The Autonomous Adversarial Loop: Fully Automating an Octo Tempest Purple-Team Simulation
talks.abstract: We are Microsoft Security Research’s Purple Team. Every simulation replays a real adversary end-to-end against production-grade defenses, then measures what our detections caught and missed. It is high signal, but slow: each run takes a skilled operator days end-to-end. So, we automated the whole loop. An infrastructure agent stands up the target environment, an autonomous red agent runs the full Octo Tempest (Scattered Spider) kill chain, and a blue agent correlates every attack step against Defender XDR to score what was detected and missed. It worked better than we expected, and it got things wrong in ways that matter. The red agent executed all 10 phases in about 45 minutes with roughly 77% verified success and zero interventions. This talk is the engineering reality of a fully autonomous purple-team loop: the architecture, the run, the metrics, and the failure modes you hit, plus the verification patterns we are adding to fix it.

talks.title: Models vs Cyber Reality: Frontier Agents Against Our Own Privately Disclosed Zero-Days
talks.abstract: Model Benchmarks say frontier agents can hack and patch. We benchmarked that against cyber reality: GPT6 Astra, Fable 5.1 and GLM5.3 vs zero-days our team found and privately disclosed in the confidential compute stack, plus 209 known vulnerabilities On the zero-days, eight agents ran 54 attempts. 12 built a working exploit. Zero produced an accepted patch. Three Chinese models took 7 of the 12 working exploits. GPT-6 Astra refused. Claude Fable 5.1 refused. We show the practical reality board and the refusal-adjusted capability board and explain 3 tasks in detail. On the known vulns, three agents each attacked and repaired the same 209 vulns. Two out of three were better attackers than defenders, when discounting shallow patches or patches that break the CI. The failures we found: A fix that refused 40% of valid messages. A patch that locked every user out.

talks.title: Secure Product Development With Mantis

speakers.name: Nick Galloway
speakers.affiliation: AI for security and security for AI, Google Cloud

speakers.name: Ruchi Shah
speakers.affiliation: Senior Director, Security Engineering, Google Cloud

talks.abstract: We detail how we have rebuilt our security engineering function around collaborative secure development. We will explain the background of starting with Mantis for vulnerability discovery and how that led to a complete reimagining of how security and software development teams collaborate to launch products.

talks.title: Your Harness Needs a Security Constitution
talks.abstract: I’ve spent years finding cloud security bugs, before and after AI, so I know how hard they are to find and how bad models are at finding them. I set out to try to fix that. The result has been 90+ valid, cloud-specific issues across multiple providers, supported by a new methodology — AI-led hunting with a Security Constitution. Models already handle finding code-level bugs like SQLi and XSS well, but these issues have never intrigued me. Instead, I tend to focus on platform-design flaws: missing authorization checks, inadequate logging, mishandled data, where I find the frontier models are much weaker. Enter a new way of hunting: the Security Constitution, modeled on Anthropic’s Ethical Constitution, is a set of 12 principles for how trust is held across multi-tenant platforms. It gives every hunt a point of view and a way to means-test a finding: the “reasonable customer test.” The principles are the worldview, and what pours out are new shapes of novel cloud vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Opened Is Not Fixed: The Last Mile of AI Vulnerability Remediation
talks.abstract: AI-assisted security programs can generate more vulnerability candidates and patch pull requests than engineering teams can review. Anthropic’s Glasswing update reports that a high or critical bug found by Mythos Preview takes two weeks to patch on average. Once discovery is cheap, review and closure are the scarce resource, and an opened pull request is an intermediate state. This field report covers the operating loop we built to move work from verified finding to merge, rejection, deferral, or formal risk acceptance: root-cause deduplication, reachability-first ranking, typed refutation reasons, explicit ownership, detector replay, and refusal to auto-patch bug classes that cannot be validated cheaply. I will show why a passing build does not prove the vulnerable path is gone and how PR volume can hide the review bottleneck. Attendees get a closure-state schema, a patch-gating checklist, and a public-target walkthrough that keep opened, reviewed, and fixed as separate states.

talks.title: 0-Click Remote Exploits in an AI World
talks.abstract: 0-click vulnerabilities in mobile messaging applications are often treated as rare, highly bespoke findings. Our experience suggests something different: with the right tooling and models remote attack surface can be enumerated and audited automatically by LLMs. This talk presents the tooling and techniques we developed for rapidly identifying and auditing remotely reachable attack surface across mobile messaging applications. We demonstrate the approach through tree concrete case studies: WeWorm, a worm that spreads through WeChat and jumps between modern iOS and Android devices, a Samsung-only WhatsApp 0click and a semi universal iOS 1click. Finally, we examine what happens as this kind of research becomes easier to automate. We discuss how scalable 0-click discovery changes the security assumptions behind messaging apps, where existing trust boundaries break down, and what application and platform vendors can do to reduce remotely exposed attack surface before these techniques become commonplace.
