Weightless: Abliteration Without the Weights
talks.abstract: Abliterating an open-weight model normally means editing and redistributing tens or hundreds of gigabytes of weights. Weightless takes a different approach: extract the behavioral direction and apply it at inference time, leaving the base checkpoint byte-identical. I’ll show how projective activation steering can suppress refusal using compact GLP artifacts (for example, a 478 KB vector for DeepSeek V4 Flash) and how the same intervention can be expressed as a rank-1 LoRA on compatible dense architectures. The underlying runtime method is not limited to dense models: it also applies to mixture-of-experts architectures such as GLM, where activation-space intervention is the more natural deployment mechanism. We’ll cover real measurements across DeepSeek, Qwen, and GLM models on DGX Spark, including refusal reduction, capability and benign-behavior gates, quantization behavior, deployment constraints, and the cases where steering breaks.

talks.title: Cryptography Under AI Pressure

speakers.name: Sunghyeon Jo
speakers.affiliation: Co-founder & Cybersecurity Researcher, QED Audit; Ph.D. student, Georgia Institute of Technology

talks.abstract: LLMs are contesting cryptography, hard. I found a signing-key recovery attack on TALUS v4, a threshold ML-DSA proposal previewed for NIST’s threshold call, using LLM harness. The authors fixed it in v5. I also broke a witness encryption scheme with a polynomial-time message recovery attack, using ChatGPT. On the Poseidon hash, four independent cryptanalysis papers landed within a month, and I got $10K ex gratia for my submission. Meanwhile, LLM autoresearch made proving other hashes like SHA faster, which decreases the need for Poseidon. And Ethereum is moving L1 off Poseidon toward SHA and BLAKE. I also proved which Reed-Solomon parameters are actually safe for SNARK soundness, and now AI autoresearch is driving all of this. With LLMs, more efficient cryptography will emerge and will be contested super hard, and only the safe ones will survive.

talks.title: Harness
Same Score, Different Brain: Comparing Models by How They Process What They Know
talks.abstract: Capability evaluation treats the model as a black box. Prompt it, harness it, score what comes out. That approach systematically understates what models know, and it tells you nothing about how they know it. This talk measures capability layer by layer. Instead of scoring output tokens, we probe internal activations at each layer to map where different types of information emerge, concentrate, and deteriorate as computation moves through the model. That layerwise map becomes a comparison tool: two models with similar benchmark scores can process identical information in structurally different ways, and those differences show where each model is robust, brittle, or degrading. We present a repeatable methodology for layerwise analysis, comparisons across model families, architectures, and parameter counts, and the effect of post-training including quantization on where capability signal lives and whether it survives. No prior mechanistic interpretability background required!

talks.title: Math Ability has Consequences — AI Cryptanalysis

speakers.name: Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen
speakers.affiliation: Cryptographer, Hardware Architect, Professor of Practice

talks.abstract: Codebreaking with AI: Techniques, recent results, and reactions from security authorities. A cryptographer breaks down how security assurances of post-quantum cryptography are holding up and which parts might break next.

talks.title: PyRIT CTF Workshop

speakers.name: Richard Lundeen
speakers.affiliation: AI Red Team Automation Lead, Microsoft

speakers.name: Behnam Ousat
speakers.affiliation: Software Engineer, Microsoft AI Red Team

talks.abstract: Participants use PyRIT in a CTF-style workshop to automate evaluations of prompt injection, jailbreaks, multi-turn attacks, and AI agent tool use.
talks.details: Description: In this two-hour hands-on workshop, participants will use PyRIT to test the security of vulnerable AI systems in a CTF-style environment. We’ll begin by manually exploring prompt injection and jailbreak challenges, then show how PyRIT can automate similar techniques at scale and in situations that have more real-world impact. Participants will learn the core PyRIT workflows and apply them against various realistic scenarios like bypassing simple defenses, multi-turn attacks, indirect prompt injection, and attacks against AI agents and tool use. The emphasis is on practical experimentation rather than lecture. By the end of the workshop, participants should understand how PyRIT turns individual adversarial prompts into repeatable, measurable AI security evaluations and how these techniques can be applied to their own systems. Prerequisites – None Participant Setup Requirements – TBD

talks.title: Reinforcement Learning for Open-Weight Security LLMs, with a Live Training Run

speakers.name: Sahil Garg
speakers.affiliation: Principal AI Researcher, Averlon | Training LLMs for Cybersecurity

talks.abstract: Hands-on workshop on reinforcement learning for security LLMs, featuring live Gemma 4 12B training to reduce over-refusal without enabling harmful requests.
talks.details: Description: In our benchmarks, open-weight LLMs match closed models on most security tasks at far lower cost, and reinforcement learning (RL) makes them task experts. This hands-on workshop teaches RL through security examples: vulnerability discovery, penetration testing and detection engineering. An LLM judge, serving as the reward model, accepts or rejects samples; accepted ones join a growing training pool. If most are rejected, iterative self-refinement improves them; failing that, a stronger open model or human annotations seed the pool. Verifiers are slower, so each round trains on judge-accepted samples, but only verified samples stay in the pool, since judges can be gamed. Adapting sampling and the reward model keeps training stable. In our experiments, many complicated RL methods proved unnecessary, and some failed outright. The live case study targets over-refusal: safety-tuned LLMs sometimes decline authorized penetration testing. Abliteration, which strips refusal from the weights, is a poor fix: in our tests it was unreliable on reasoning models and hurt capability, and it disarms refusals for attackers too. Instead, RL retrains Gemma 4 12B live to help with authorized work while still refusing harmful requests. Participants red-team each checkpoint as a dashboard tracks false refusals and harmful compliance. Prerequisites: A coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode; our skill files let it build and run the labs. No machine-learning, RL or model-training experience needed. Helpful: penetration-testing or other security experience. ML practitioners new to security are equally welcome. Participant Setup Requirements: A laptop with a coding agent such as Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode. No GPU needed. Lab files and endpoint access, sent in advance with a short setup check.

talks.title: You Ran Mythos and Grew the Queue. Now What? Who Fixes These Security Issues?

speakers.name: Kamal Srinivasan
speakers.affiliation: Co-founder, UnitOne | Building security remediation for enterprise teams

talks.abstract: A practical walkthrough of prioritizing vulnerabilities, locating and testing fixes with a coding agent, meeting reporting obligations, and deciding what to release.
talks.details: Description: The scanner found a real vulnerability. Engineering needs to know where to change the code, whether the fix will break anything, and how to get it into customers’ hands. Meanwhile, security has another hundred findings to work through. This workshop follows one issue through that process. Starting with a sample application and a mixed queue of findings, we’ll decide what needs attention, identify the affected code and configuration, and use a coding agent to propose a fix. We’ll inspect the patch, test it, and work through what happens when it fails. We’ll also cover the EU Cyber Resilience Act: when a finding needs to be reported, who owns that decision, and why a reporting deadline is different from a patch deadline. PCI requirements and customer commitments provide other examples of how priorities get set. The exercise ends with a release decision and a record of what was fixed, what was tested, and what remains exposed. No Mythos access is needed. Prerequisites: Basic familiarity with vulnerability findings, Git pull requests and CI/CD. Participants should be comfortable reading simple application code and running terminal commands. No prior CRA expertise or Mythos access is required. Participant Setup Requirements: A laptop with Git, Docker and a code editor. Download the workshop repository and container images before the session. Access to an AI coding assistant; a prepared-output path will let participants complete the exercises without a paid account. Use only the supplied lab application and synthetic data.

talks.title: Coffee break
Coffee break
There Isn’t a Security Problem an Agent Can’t Help Solve
talks.abstract: Security reviews often create a chronic bottleneck, leaving developers waiting while specialists manually gather context. To eliminate this friction, we built AI agents at Stripe that manage the end-to-end security lifecycle – from initial context gathering and threat modeling to ticket creation, risk tracking, and fix verification. With scoped authority and evidence-based outputs so human experts can focus on complex, high-risk architectural decisions. This transitions manual prep to self-service workflows cut our reviews from weeks to minutes. In this talk, we’ll share practical deployment lessons and a repeatable framework for identifying agent-worthy security workflows that enhance, rather than replace, expert human judgment. You’ll leave with a repeatable framework for identifying agent-worthy security problems and designing loops that enhance expert judgment. This helps security teams from managing a queue to focusing on higher-order safety challenges.

talks.title: Kuna: Building a Competitive C Decompiler Through Autonomous AI Research
talks.abstract: At the core of every computing system is compiled code known as binaries. Decompilers turn binaries into source-like code, helping researchers and AI agents analyze software without its source. Despite decades of research, compilation’s information loss leaves decompilers dependent on expert-built heuristics that don’t scale. Can agents develop better decompilation methods, rather than just use existing tools? I present Kuna, an experiment extending my PhD research by giving agents a dataset, a problem space, and a platform to improve. Starting from Ghidra, we ported the decompiler to Rust, made its passes tunable, and built loops for agents to investigate failures and evaluate new methods. Within three months, Kuna reached a 33.7% perfect rate on C control flow structure versus Hex-Rays’ 32.2% on DecBench (33k samples). I’ll show agent-developed methods, compare decompilation, and explain where autonomy worked, where human direction helped, and how it’s changing modern research.

talks.title: Metrics for Agentic Systems: What “Good” Looks Like for a Security Agent
talks.abstract: Teams are shipping AI security agents faster than they can answer a basic question: is it actually working well? This talk draws on building metrics programs across multiple production security agents — triage, threat intel, and detection workloads — to show what “good” means for an agentic system in practice. I’ll cover turning existing human-in-the-loop workflows into feedback signal, defining metrics that go beyond accuracy (throughput, guardrail integrity, trust), and what changes when you move from “can we measure this” to “can we trust this number.”

talks.title: Two Sparks Walk Into a Lab
talks.abstract: I asked an AI coding agent to help me build a red-team benchmark on two NVIDIA DGX Sparks I’d never configured before. 33 open-weight models later: willingness to answer an offensive-security question and getting it right are different axes. One abliterated model correctly diagnosed a planted false-positive in a BloodHound attack path – then recommended re-enabling the disabled account it had just flagged as safe, contradicting its own analysis. This talk covers building a red-team-specific harness (a hand-authored answer key, a deliberate false-positive trap) from zero prior GPU-cluster experience – directing an AI agent through the deployment while personally verifying what mattered, and what that verification actually looked like. It covers the hardware findings (architecture beats parameter count on memory-bandwidth-limited hardware), the correctness spread across 33 models, and an honest answer to whether local hardware is worth it for offensive work.

talks.title: The Scanner Said Clean. We Ran It Again: Stochastic False Negatives in LLM Vulnerability Detection
talks.abstract: An LLM vulnerability scanner can miss a real bug on one run and find it on the next without signaling uncertainty. We measured this failure in 25,000 trials across 50 models on a benchmark selected for on-and-off detection. A separate 7,600-run study tested rediscovery of 95 disclosed CVEs in OpenSSL, curl, GnuTLS and five other heavily audited projects. The results challenge the usual “pick the strongest model” strategy: repeated passes help, but diverse inexpensive models cover complementary blind spots and outperform a costlier single model. We will show our open-source scanner finding – and missing – the same bug, reveal which intuitive pipeline additions failed to justify their cost, and examine the gap between broadly detectable JS and PHP bugs and stubbornly hard stateful C vulnerabilities. Attendees will learn how to measure cumulative detection, compare complementary coverage and identify cases needing other techniques, using the public benchmark, harness and scanner.

talks.title: Hidden Triggers, Harmful Payloads: Auditing Trojan Open-Weight LLMs
talks.abstract: Open-weight models are increasingly important. Guardrails on frontier models affect cybersecurity research are pushing us toward open-weight LLMs. But are you sure the quant you downloaded is safe? Trojan models remain largely theoretical because they are difficult to identify. Triggers may be a date, codebase, environment, or pattern; malicious behaviour may include injecting vulnerable code, overlooking vulnerabilities, or favouring a dependency. An unknown trigger and payload create a challenging problem. Most supervised fine-tuning methods for creating Trojans miss triggers, break normal tasks, or leak payloads without a trigger. We developed a robust pipeline for realistic Trojan models with specific, effective triggers that preserve standard capabilities. Using a zoo of Trojan models, we test methods from linear probes to J-space across triggers, payloads, model sizes, and architectures. Our results provide a foundation for detecting and mitigating Trojans in open-weight LLMs.

talks.title: Offense != Defense: LLM Cyber Defense – Hunt, Bust, Climb

speakers.name: Igor Kozlov
speakers.affiliation: AI/ML Lead, Staff Applied Scientist, Simibian.ai

talks.abstract: Offense != defense. Models that excel at vulnerability finding fail at open-ended threat hunting – our receipts show these are distinct skills. We evaluate LLMs on campaigns built from 105 real attack procedures spanning 13 of 14 ATT&CK tactics. Each hunt contains ~100,000 logs with deterministic behavior-level ground truth. No model met the ≥50%-recall-on-every-tactic passing rule; leading coverage was 45.1%. Results busted myths from non-domain-specific benchmarks. Traces exposed misalignment – agentsplaining and resource guardrails bypass – and operational flaws – evidence that a raw LLM agent cannot be trusted to autonomously perform open-ended defensive threat hunting. We provide practical harness-engineering recommendations and demonstrate a prompt-level self-improvement loop in our dense-reward RL gym, raising Kimi 2.6 from 13.4% to 18.7% coverage. This suggests that LLM defense capabilities are trainable – and that defense, not offense, should be the training target.

talks.title: OH MODEL, WHERE ART THOU: Hacking Chrome’s Local SLM
talks.abstract: With the inclusion of a Gemini-class local language model in Google Chrome, endpoints finally have a local model and inference engine deployed at scale. With all the possibilities that this brings comes also new attack surfaces. In this talk, the audience will learn about how Chrome’s local model details, its integration into Safe Browsing, how the local inference APIs are reachable by any website and how that could be abused for new traffic monetization schemes through a token-farming botnet, and how malware could sideload the local model and use local inference to power itself as it worms through a network.

talks.title: Lunch break
Lunch break
Lunch break
Towards Monitoring Too Cheap To Meter: Jev Monitor Escalation For Real time Scope Enforcement
talks.abstract: Agents have scaled up software development and are doing the same for cybersecurity. Capabilities have superseded alignment. For software, there has been an increased focus on sandboxing techniques to prevent agents from doing any harm to development environments and infrastructure. Security has no such luxury. As such, higher-risk fields like network operations lag behind in producing an agentic workforce. Put simply: we cannot trust agents to stay in scope while completing their objectives. Monitoring systems both probabilistic and deterministic are released every day, often without an understanding of the latency, token, and capability cost imposed on the agents they monitor. To understand those tradeoffs and better prepare for production, we need to make those numbers legible. To this end, we introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark of tasks broken into capability and scope adherence tests. This allows for testing different monitoring solutions to see how they affect safety in an apples-to-apples comparison, as well as whether they affect capability. To illustrate how ScopeBench can be used this way, we look at multiple synchronous monitoring schemes on top of a basic agentic harness: Jev-based decision model only, LLM-as-a-judge only, and an escalation cascade where Jev is run as a cheap first pass, escalating to a more powerful model when necessary.

talks.title: Built to Spec, Ignored in Practice: Rebuilding AI Intake People Actually Use

speakers.name: Olivia Rose
speakers.affiliation: Co-Founder, Williams Rose AI Cyber Advisory

speakers.name: Kayla Williams
speakers.affiliation: Co-Founder, Williams Rose AI Cyber Advisory

talks.abstract: We’re two former CISOs. A large pharma company brought us a puzzle: their AI intake and risk-tiering process was live and built to spec, yet almost no one used it. Twenty submissions in six months. We pulled the logs. In one 24-hour sample, we found 35 AI unapproved cases already running across the org. Here’s the uncomfortable part. Their v1 was the industry-standard GRC playbook: vendor-risk forms, tiered classification, committee review. The team was competent. We’d have built the same thing. But our experience rolling out AI programs told us where it broke down. The org needed controls, yes, but the real fix was cultural. AI use cases come from people who’ve never filed a risk request and never had to. This talk covers the diagnosis data, v1 and v2 rubrics side by side, and the rebuilt workflow: self-service fast lanes for low tiers, human review only where warranted, plus a sanitized walkthrough of the intake tooling. Attendees leave with both rubrics and redesign criteria.

talks.title: Defense
Playing Games and Making Decisions with AI

speakers.name: Richard Johnson
speakers.affiliation: Fuzzing IO and Metaframe AI, advanced cybersecurity and agent solutions

talks.abstract: A workshop on non-generative AI, covering classifiers, embeddings, reinforcement learning, probabilistic decision models, and applications in workflows, games, and business logic.
talks.details: Description: The world of AI hype cycles is typically dominated by the latest generative AI trends: new chatbots, image and video generators, coding agents, and synthetic music. But just a few weeks ago, Diogo Almeida, a co-creator of ChatGPT, launched a new model series called Jev that doesn’t generate text or images. Instead, it makes fast, probabilistic decisions over defined choices, producing answers that software can act on directly, igniting a renewed interest in the many other forms of AI that most have not been exposed to. This workshop will focus on the others. The non-generative AI world. We will explore purpose-built tiny models, general models adapted to domain-specific tasks, classifiers, embedding and similarity models, reinforcement learning systems, the emerging class of Jev-like decision models, and yes, even a synthetic reconstruction of a fly’s neurological connectome playing games and driving decisions and outcomes. Over the course of two hours we will learn about model training, classifiers, reinforcement learning, and how to apply what seems like fun and games to navigating workflows and desision trees in arbitrary business logic and even extending the ability of more generalized LLM agents with new super powers. Join us as we explore the fascinating world of non-generative AI, the unspoken, scalable powerhouse of AI that has been silently driving businesses processes globally for decades. Prerequisites: Python programming ability will be required to complete exercises, however observers or management will also see value in understanding a new range of applications for AI. Skeleton code or working demos will be provided that participants can use as-is or expand upon according to skill level. Participant Setup Requirements: SSH to a cloud server is minimum requirement.

talks.title: Vibe Coding an Evasion Framework [SANS]
talks.abstract: Hands-on workshop on building a containerized shellcode-to-C# loader framework with AI assistance and verifying configurable evasion techniques against MITRE ATT&CK.
talks.details: Description: AI coding assistants collapse the time between “I need a tool for this” and having one running, but only if you use them well. Asking a model for a whole application at once reliably produces hallucinated APIs, incoherent architecture, and code you don’t understand well enough to trust. This hands-on workshop teaches a “think then act” methodology for AI-assisted security tool development, using a custom payload evasion framework as the vehicle. Attendees prompt an assistant to produce a Product Requirements Document, review and correct that design against authoritative references, then implement in small, verifiable phases. The result is a containerized web application that accepts raw shellcode and emits C# loaders with configurable evasion options (payload bloating, sleep delays, anti-sandbox checks, environmental keying, domain-joined validation, entropy reduction), mapping to ATT&CK T1027, T1497.001, T1480.001, and T1055. The emphasis throughout is verification over generation. Prerequisites: None Participant Setup Requirements: Participants will need a laptop capable of running an Intel x64 virtual machine. BIOS settings must be set to enable virtualization technology, such as “Intel-VTx” or “AMD-V” extensions. Administrator / root access required 8GB of RAM Mac laptops are only permitted if they use Intel processors, rather than Apple M-series CPUs

talks.title: Possession Is Not Permission: Hands-On Authority Control for Capable Agents

speakers.name: Sung Whan Moon
speakers.affiliation: Head of Partnership and Operations, Mirror Security

talks.abstract: Hands-on workshop on destination-side authority verification for agents, using signed goals, narrowing delegation, action digests, leases, and state-bound receipts to reject credential misuse.
talks.details: Description: Agents are getting better at finding another route. In July 2026, about 700 benchmark agents coordinated through a shared package registry, recovered credentials and crossed into a real third-party service. Nobody jailbroke them. The tasks were impossible, the goal stayed active, and every system on the path accepted a working credential as permission. This workshop teaches one control that holds when the model, sandbox and monitor all miss: the system that commits a consequence verifies the original authority, not just a valid token. You start with a small agent harness and a mock destination that trusts bearer tokens. You break it with five attacks drawn from real incidents: goal substitution, credential retargeting, threshold splitting, delegation expansion and a compaction summary claiming approval. Then you build the check that stops them: a signed root goal, delegation that can only narrow, an exact action digest, a short-lived lease and a receipt tied to the destination’s real state. The approved work keeps running. The expanded action does not. The kit is vendor-neutral Python built on familiar primitives (Macaroons, HTTP Message Signatures, Cedar-style policy). You leave with the repo, a worksheet and a checklist to apply to your own agents on Monday. Prerequisites: Comfort reading and editing Python. Basic familiarity with HTTP APIs and what a bearer token is. No prior agent-security or cryptography background needed: the kit supplies the signing and policy primitives and every step is guided by a test. Participant Setup Requirements: A laptop with Python 3.11+ (or Docker Desktop), git and a terminal. Before the session: clone the repository from the link we send out and run the one-line setup so dependencies are cached; a USB copy may be available in the room. No accounts, cloud resources, GPU or API keys are required. Optional: an API key for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint if you want to run the live-model lane instead of the recorded one.

talks.title: What Designing a Cyber Ontology for Agents Taught Us About Governance

speakers.name: David Chismon
speakers.affiliation: Chief Security Architect, The UK National Cyber Security Centre

talks.abstract: The UK is building CyberShield, a national-scale agentic cyber defence ecosystem, a 5 year plan to both agentify existing cyber efforts as well as enable entirely novel ones. As part of the early research, we have been researching how we can codify cyber security information as a knowledge graph to aid deterministic decision making. The process of doing so produced unexpected benefits – new understanding of controls, risk, and impact. Pulling on these threads has lead to potential new approaches in how you might design compliance regimes and make governance significantly more effective, in a way that scales with increasing numbers of agentic workloads to consider, rather than becoming strained. This talk will cover the research, the approach, the findings, and what it might mean for governance.

talks.title: Permission Fatigue Is a Security Bug: Dynamic Guardrails for Coding Agents

speakers.name: Chris Puderbaugh
speakers.affiliation: Security Engineer – Agent Security & Access, Meta

talks.abstract: Agents don’t need novel attacks to create novel risk:they collapse the distance between untrusted input and privileged action, giving ordinary techniques reach and scale. Per-action approval made it worse: people approved reflexively or disabled checks. Past a volume threshold, friction is not a security control; it is a control failure. We replaced static gates with a runtime separating three concerns most agent security models fuse. Signals: a sidecar records untrusted reads into a store where taint accumulates and cannot be cleared. Policy: rules live outside the agent, bounded by an agent role in a signed X509 attribute. Decision: a cheapest-first cascade of static rules, stateful checks, LLM classifier returns allow, ask, or deny. Access tightens mid-session as taint accrues; At 100% guardrail rollout, friction fell 80% retaining security. What failed: allowlists right per population and wrong per workflow, provenance filtering too coarse to block, subagent propagation still open.

talks.title: Memory Is the New Attack Surface: Benchmarking Poisoning Through Agent Memory
talks.abstract: Memory is a core capability of AI agents, and it creates a new attack surface. A single poisoned tool response can persist beyond the session that delivered it, be rewritten into new memories, reappear during later benign tasks, and only then drive the attacker’s objective. This delayed failure makes memory poisoning both consequential and difficult to diagnose. To identify which memory implementations are most resistant, and understand why, we need a benchmark that follows attacks through the full memory lifecycle. Memory Dojo provides that capability, tracing storage, transformation, retrieval, propagation, and downstream behavior across five distinct memory architectures. The result is a practical way to compare resistance, explain where defenses hold or fail, and determine whether an agent that appears safe now has already been poisoned to fail later.

talks.title: Your AI Analyst Is Confidently Wrong: Adversarial QC for Agentic Security Analysis

speakers.name: Maxim Kovalsky
speakers.affiliation: Managing Director, AI Security CoE, Consortium Networks, Consortium

talks.abstract: Agentic workflows are moving into cybersecurity work humans can’t verify at the volume agents produce it. A GRC assessment, architecture review, or threat model can run to thousands of claims. Nobody has time to check every one. We built a harness to do the checking. Every claim is a structured unit a machine can test, with deterministic gates as the hard authority. An adversarial critic reviews what the gates cannot, under rules that stop it inventing findings; a fixer corrects until the work converges or gets flagged. We measure accuracy, regression per pass, omissions, and cost. It came from two builds: a production QC loop for AI security vendor research, and a benchmark scoring frontier and leading open weight models on ATT&CK coverage mapping. Human judgment goes in once: an answer key proving the harness grades correctly. We’ll show failure modes, including fixes that make work worse, and how to adapt it to tasks of similar cognitive complexity.

talks.title: PHPocalypse: Finding, Exploiting, and Disclosing php2shell
talks.abstract: What does AI miss, and how do experienced vulnerability researchers fill the gaps? Through the story of php2shell, we show how deep knowledge of a target and exploitation techniques helps human researchers guide AI, uncover vulnerabilities, and turn crashes into working exploits. Then comes the inevitable question: how do you disclosure when a vulnerability affects an enormous ecosystem? We share the difficult decisions, mistakes, and lessons from our attempt. We don’t think the process worked particularly well, and we don’t have a tidy answer for how to do it better.

talks.title: Pandora’s Dir – Hope at the bottom of ../
talks.abstract: Everyone is speculating about how threat actors are using AI behind the scenes, but this telemetry is notoriously hard to come by. Unless however, threat actors leave their servers wide open. Armed with a scaled and targeted open-directory pipeline plus the hypothesis that exposed infrastructure holds the real story, we went hunting for the intersection of malicious activity and AI adoption. This presentation will jump into our findings, rabbit holes, time sinks, and that of a rainbow donkey. We’ll share qualitative real-world cases about weaponized AI assistants, an AI agent running an underground syndicate, and 23K hoarded API keys. We will break down our analysis and the trends we observed when cracking open these digital Pandora’s boxes. While we discovered mature AI setups for malicious use cases, we came to the conclusion that, at least for now, there is hope at the bottom of ../

talks.title: Coffee break
Coffee break
Claude Can Capture the Flag. Can It Hold the Fort?
talks.abstract: Imagine being dropped into a company at 8 a.m. with the network already on fire. Attackers are inside, the business wants to know whether payroll still works, and the CEO keeps emailing for incident reports. That’s the Collegiate Cyber Defense Competition (CCDC). For four months we ran autonomous Claude agents as a blue team through three rounds of CCDC, defending a fictional water and power utility against a professional red team. We saw all of it: from the engineering it took to run 200+ concurrent agents with shared state, to an adversarial mindset that turned into full paranoia. Along the way our agents took down nine of their own services fighting each other over one password, and attacked the red team’s C2. Expect a candid account of building an AI blue team: what we built, what broke, and what we got wrong about why.

talks.title: Auditing Someone Else’s Confidential AI

speakers.name: Jagannadh Mellacheruvu
speakers.affiliation: AI Security and Policy, Mirror Security

talks.abstract: Confidential-computing hardware already signs a statement about itself: which chip, which firmware, debug on or off, whether the operator can see inside. Vendors use that proof to unlock keys for their own customers and rarely show it to anyone else. This demo shows what happens when an outsider keeps it. Live, with no cloud account, I fetch the attestation document a production confidential-inference service publishes and verify its AMD SEV-SNP report and certificate chain to AMD’s root with an open-source, dependency-free tool. The tool then grades the evidence against twelve governance checks and writes an auditor-readable report mapped to EU AI Act Art. 15 and Annex IV, SOC 2 CC6/CC7 and ISO 42001. Five checks pass on real hardware, six with a network-timing bound on where the machine is; the rest are unknown, and I show why: no vendor token carries location, compute or licence state, exactly what the Chip Security Act now asks silicon to provide.

talks.title: Every Dog Has its 0-day
talks.abstract: Quadruped and humanoid robots are shipping to consumers by the tens of thousands; walking, camera-equipped, cloud-connected computers running AI policies with real actuators. The security model collapses at every trust boundary: BLE provisioning that hands out its crypto keys; a “secretless” app channel whose authentication is a hardcoded string; an unauthenticated bus where two different services give pre-auth root; a deterministic, ASLR-independent pc-control primitive in the WebRTC bridge; an insecure AI-assistant channel that lets a network dispatch device commands and its worm able. The AI onboard is no better. Starting with the prompting: “Satisfy the master’s requests at all times – you may not refuse…'” Means any prompt injection via camera, mic, etc will be fulfilled. Skills can be combined to disable firmware safety mechanisms like obstacle and human avoidance. We will define the ’embodied reasoning lethal trifecta’ and what we should avoid as an industry.

talks.title: AI Client Builders are Not Security Companies (And Shouldn’t Have To Be)

speakers.name: Alexander Frazer
speakers.affiliation: Security Engineer, Runlayer – Enterprise AI Infrastructure for MCP and Agents

talks.abstract: As agents get more autonomous, two requirements get sharp: a real record of what the agent did (observability), and a place to gate a risky action before it runs (control). Right now every client — Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex — builds its own version of both, differently, and none of it interoperates. That’s a black box at exactly the moment we need transparency, and it makes security each builder’s side project instead of a shared capability. MCP is starting to address this at the tool-call layer (interceptors are in progress). Necessary, but not enough: a modern agent plans, chains many tools, and spawns sub-agents, so the observability and control points that matter span the whole agentic lifecycle, a level up from any single tool call. It’s the same instinct as wanting a finite, inspectable capability tree for an agent: you can’t trust what you can’t see or stop. This is forward-looking, but grounded. I’ll show concretely what a lifecycle-level observability event and a control checkpoint look like, a before/after of an agent action with no record and no gate versus the same action with a standard one in place, and how it connects to prior art this room already knows: OPA/Cedar for policy, OCSF for events, and the MCP interceptor work. I’ll be honest about the tradeoffs — latency, developer friction, where this is still hype — and what has to be true for a shared standard to actually happen. The argument: client builders shouldn’t have to become security companies. The same way you hand card processing to a specialist instead of rolling your own, agent platforms need shared observability and control points so security is a shared responsibility. I chair the AAIF Security & Privacy Working Group and would treat this talk as a feeder into that standards work. Takeaways: the two control points that matter as autonomy increases, how they sit above MCP, and where the real engineering tradeoffs are.

talks.title: Agents Attacking Agents: A Hands-On CTF in Red Teaming Agentic Systems.
talks.abstract: Hands-on CTF on using attacker agents to red team chatbots, multi-agent systems, and AI infrastructure while measuring attack success and building robust evaluations.
talks.details: Description: The fastest way to test an AI agent is to point another agent at it. This workshop is a hands-on, competitive CTF where participants use attacker agents to red team live targets: single agents, multi-agent systems, and infrastructure. In this workshop, participants work through a scored challenge set. They start by driving an attacker agent against a chatbot to exfiltrate data, then move to multi-agent systems where they try to influence a swarm of agents, and lastly, they use agents to perform a pentest on a mix of traditional and AI infrastructure. Participants will also learn to score attacker-agent output at scale, measure attack success rate across repeated runs, and build evaluations that can’t be easily cheated by agents. Prerequisites: Working knowledge of security fundamentals. A general understanding of how agents work. Participant Setup Requirements: A laptop with a current web browser and Wi-Fi A GitHub, Gmail, or Outlook account to access the CTF (Optional) Virtual machine to run red teaming agents and tools.

talks.title: Auto-Exploiter by Use of a Ratchet Loop, Code Understanding, and… Haiku
talks.abstract: We built an exploit-generation system using Anthropic’s Haiku model. Our first approach was a Karpathy-style auto-research loop with a progressive ratchet, using Opus. It was only with Opus 4.7 that the model started producing useful results. That led to a second insight: the limiting factor was whether the system actually understood code. And with Opus, the engineering problem became too easy. Making the system work with Haiku became our badge of honor: endless failure. Haiku tends to favor fast responses, avoid extended reasoning, and avoid tool use. We focused on the harness again: how it represents the target, preserves state, reasons about code paths, tracks vulnerability conditions, and carries exploitation progress across attempts. The hardest cases still fail. We have not yet achieved full exploitation of difficult real-world memory corruption targets (Baron Samedit and libwebp) with mitigations. We made real progress, and we’re here to share our many failures.

talks.title: AgencyScore and AgencyGym: Measuring Excessive Agency Before Deployment
talks.abstract: OpenAI models chained zero-days out of their own sandbox into Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. The ExploitGym team found models probing infrastructure for privilege beyond the task. No adversary was involved. Autonomous, goal-seeking agents acquire higher agency: they don’t stop at ordinary failures, they “meltdown” searching for ways to finish the task at all costs. OWASP names this Excessive Agency. Most agent security assumes an attacker manipulating a prompt. A trusted agent with approved tools can cause harm by trying too hard. We built AgencyScore to measure an agent acquiring capability it wasn’t declared to have, before deployment. AgencyGym is a sandbox with a 100-task dataset. High agency capabilities are placed as capture-the-flag tests for agents to acquire. We show agency acquisition rates, how security and red teams can use it, and where combinatorial coverage across tools and infrastructure remains incomplete. This is v1. We need community help to evolve it.

talks.title: Stolen Thoughts: How Adversaries Steal Reasoning for Industrial-Scale Distillation
Half the Model Never Multiplies: Quantizing a Reasoner for the Endpoint
talks.abstract: A data-loss classifier that phones home has to transmit the secret in order to ask whether it is one. So ours runs on the endpoint: one quantized open-weight base, and a harness serving several agents off it. Gemma-4 E2B keeps half its parameters in a lookup table read one row per token and never multiplied, so error there is additive noise rather than error compounded through a matmul chain. Three builds carrying that table at F16, Q8_0 and Q3_K_S all score 34 of 40 and fail on the same six items; the compute path meanwhile falls 39 of 40 to 34 between Q4 and Q3. So we spend bits where they multiply: 3.2 GB uniform becomes 2.1 GB. Serving flags take memory 1,137 MiB to 125 – 9.1x, at no throughput cost. Three jobs ride those bytes, same weights, different prompt: classify sensitive data at 51 ms a call; compact raw activity into a chronological narrative; score risk against that narrative, the user’s role and peer baseline. We will explain how we made it work.

talks.title: CISOs Debrief: What We Learned, What We Need
Closing Remarks
Mingling & Something sweet
Debate: Where is the Vulnpocalypse?

speakers.name: Sergej Epp
speakers.affiliation: Creator of the Zero Day Clock, Leading Infosec and Threat Research

talks.abstract: A debate between Sergej Epp, creator of the Zero Day Clock, and Jeremiah Grossman, founder of White Hat Security and current CEO of Root Evidence, about the impact of AI for threat actors and defenders, both today and in the near future. The resolution: “Resolved, that AI noise hasn’t moved the needle on current cyber risk”

talks.title: Debate: Burn Down the Playbook: Can Yesterday’s Defenses Stop Tomorrow’s Attacks?
talks.abstract: How do we build a security program to defend against agent swarms? Is this about our basics, reprioritizing controls, or something completely new and AI-flavored? Join Tim Brown and Gadi Evron as they explore the topic, and disagree on what is actually useful, today.

talks.title: Debate: Too big to jail: Do human attackers also get misalignment and act rogue?
AI Hacker Jeopardy
Gathering & Mingling
Opening Words
Move between rooms
The death of TTPs – Fully Autonomous Cyber Attacks in the Wild

speakers.name: Eyal Sela
speakers.affiliation: Director of Threat Intelligence, Gambit Security

talks.abstract: Using an open-weight model and an open-source harness, a credit-card skimmer breached dozens of companies, including multibillion-dollar businesses. Given only general objectives, AI agents autonomously achieved remote code execution and control within hours in diverse environments, from web applications to cloud infrastructure, Kubernetes clusters and deployment pipelines. The impact included hundreds of thousands of stolen payment-card records, deployed skimmers, altered production configurations and destroyed data, alongside claimed access to tens of millions of business records. In this talk, I will walk through one of the first documented large-scale criminal campaigns in which AI executed individual intrusions end to end, examining its novelty and implications for detection and TTP-based attribution.

talks.title: Hacking Truth: Forged Lean Proofs and the Risk of Verifier Bugs
talks.abstract: Bugs in provers like Lean and Rocq can let you prove 1=0 and other falsehoods. That’s nothing new. But in the age of “vericoding” the stakes have changed. How much trust should we place in machine-checked proofs and formally verified cryptographic software? We revisit seven previously reported soundness bugs in Lean and Rocq, some still unpatched. Recognizing them as security vulnerabilities, we requested and obtained seven CVEs. Exploiting these bugs, we show: – Forged proofs of P = NP, the Riemann Hypothesis, and other Millennium Prize Problems. Our proofs are deliberately short and unlikely to fool an expert human reviewer, but more elaborate and convincing forgeries could be constructed. – A sabotaged Fiat-Crypto field multiplier that always returns zero, while its original correctness theorem remains accepted. Fiat-Crypto-derived code is used by BoringSSL and other prominent projects. – We also demonstrate soundness failures in Z3, including one that makes downstream verification tools accept false claims. We provide reproducible Docker PoCs for these results. None of the prover/verifier projects appeared to have a documented security disclosure policy. It’s now time to treat them as security boundaries and prioritize fixing exploitable bugs, with proper disclosure processes, lest more false proofs and results creep into the ecosystem, accidentally or maliciously. Finally, we present a new 1911-line Rocq formalization of a constructive reduction to Rice’s theorem, concerning the undecidability of nontrivial semantic properties of programs, which got us started on this research.

talks.title: Art
‐‐Dangerously-Deploy-Sandboxes: a Story of Isolation and Alignment
talks.abstract: A bug provides a small, incomplete window into the thinking of the team that shipped it. When risk emerges from the interaction of features, that window can reveal even more: the assumptions about security and control embedded in the system’s design. This talk examines sandboxing and isolation weaknesses in a widely deployed frontier-lab product, alongside the controls intended to contain them. It traces how those features interact and explores what the design reveals about the lab’s perspectives and assumptions around security and alignment. Further details pending coordinated disclosure.

talks.title: Beyond the SBOM: Proving Process Integrity with the Open PBOM Specification

speakers.name: Aishwarya Athreya
speakers.affiliation: Cybersecurity Engineer, Application Security Architect, Visa

talks.abstract: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) standards answer one vital question: What binaries and open-source libraries are packed into this artifact? However, modern supply chain attacks—from compromise of CI runners to poisoned build dependencies—target the assembly mechanism itself. Knowing what is inside a container does not tell you how it was built, who approved the pipeline execution, or whether the build environment was tampered with in transit. The same blind spot exists for AI: an SBOM doesn’t capture what was asked of a model or what it answered. To solve this, we released the open Prompt Bill of Materials (PBOM) Specification on GitHub. The PBOM specification establishes a standardized, machine-readable schema that records LLM interactions as hash-chained, tamper-evident records, capturing identity, prompt and response fingerprints, model and inference parameters, and pre-inference commitments.

talks.title: Zero Trust for the Agentic SOC: Building, Governing, and Stress-Testing in the AI Era [SANS]

speakers.name: Ismael Valenzuela
speakers.affiliation: SANS Author and Senior Instructor, VP of Labs, Threat Research and Intelligence at Arctic Wolf

speakers.name: Greg Scheidel
speakers.affiliation: SANS Certified Instructor, Chief Cybersecurity Officer of Everforth ECS’s Cyber Division

talks.abstract: In this hands-on session, after a short briefing reconstructing a Silk Typhoon-style intrusion, you’ll build, run, and then break an AI-powered incident response system. You’ll play three roles: its designer, its supervisor, and its attacker.
talks.details: Description: An attacker phishes an OAuth consent grant, steals a Primary Refresh Token, and quietly maps partner tenants: no password cracked, no signature tripped. Detecting it is the easy part; the real question is what happens in the minutes after. Attendees sit inside an agentic incident-response pipeline as its architect, its governor, and finally its stress-tester. After a short briefing reconstructing a Silk Typhoon-style intrusion, they go hands-on with a working LangGraph workflow: normalizing raw Entra ID logs into OCSF, tracing an agent that correlates signals across identity, network, endpoint, and data layers, computing a composite risk score, and receiving a live LLM-recommended containment action. At the Human-in-the-Loop gate, each attendee must approve, override, or escalate the AI’s decision with documented justification before enforcement fires through a Policy Decision Point to Policy Enforcement Point chain against a Conditional Access API. Then they stress-test their own pipeline the way an adversary would: first holding the composite risk score just below the enforcement threshold while the intrusion proceeds, then turning the agent’s over-privileged credentials against it to tamper with the detection dataset and watch the risk score collapse. Prerequisites: None Participant Setup Requirements Participants will need a laptop capable of running an Intel x64 virtual machine. BIOS settings must be set to enable virtualization technology, such as “Intel-VTx” or “AMD-V” extensions. Administrator / root access required 8GB of RAM Mac laptops are only permitted if they use Intel processors, rather than Apple M-series CPUs

talks.title: Hacking Kubernetes Like an Agent – Hands-on With the Hugging Face Breach
talks.abstract: A hands-on workshop exploring the Kubernetes and EKS attack path involved in the Hugging Face compromise using a browser-based cyber range.
talks.details: Description: The OpenAI hack on Hugging Face has been described as the product of “machine speed,” but Hugging Face’s compromise didn’t really rely on novel techniques, speed, or zero-day vulnerabilities. The attack path is actually one you can learn to do in this short workshop, even if you’re not familiar with Kubernetes or EKS yet. Come learn about Kubernetes and get hands-on experience with the vital parts of the Hugging Face compromise’s attack path! You won’t need to set up tooling, just bring a machine with a modern browser so you can use our cyber range. Prerequisites: Participants need to be comfortable with a Linux or OS X command line interface. Kubernetes background is not required. Participant Setup Requirements: Participants will need a browser, but nothing else. Please ensure that your registration included an e-mail address that we can use to send you links during the event.

talks.title: Your Agent’s Approval Prompt Is an Attack Surface. Gate It.
talks.abstract: Install and red-team SP1 Gate, an open-source Claude Code control that tests risky actions with deterministic questions and measures detection versus false alarms.
talks.details: Description: Human-in-the-loop is the control everyone cites for agent safety, and in practice it is a person pressing 1. Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts. OWASP’s Agentic Top 10 calls the result ASI09, human-agent trust exploitation: a fluent agent, a tired reviewer, and a malicious action waved through. Slopsquatted packages, a secrets file swept into a commit, a shell command built from user input, an instruction planted in a ticket: each passes the same prompt. SP1 Gate is an open-source control for that step. It hooks into Claude Code and holds a risky action until the human answers factual questions about what it will do, with answer keys computed deterministically from the parsed command and the code’s syntax tree, out of band from the model. A compromised agent cannot answer its own quiz. In two hours, you will install the gate, drive six attack-shaped prompts through it, write and test a detection rule for a command it currently misses, then red-team it: as the agent, try to get a risky action past the gate, and file what works. We close by measuring the control itself, hit rate against seeded malicious proposals versus false alarms, so you can say what it caught. Prerequisites: Comfortable in a terminal basic Python (you can read a function and write an if statement) have used an AI coding agent at least once. Participant Setup Requirements: Before arriving: Laptop with Python 3.9 or later (macOS and Linux tested Windows users should use WSL). Claude Code installed and signed in (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise or Console account); confirm Claude starts before you arrive. git and a clone of github.com/ritasabri/sp1-gate A browser that can open pages served from 127.0.0.1.

talks.title: Coffee break
Coffee break
What 40 Enterprises Who Asked for Agent Governance Had, and the Control Plane That Came Out of

speakers.name: Josh Woodruff
speakers.affiliation: Founder and CEO, MassiveScale.AI , and Founding Chair, Agentic Trust Framework at CSAI Foundation

talks.abstract: Since January I’ve sat in 40-plus hour-long sessions with enterprise security teams asking how to govern AI agents: banks, insurers, hospitals, a railroad, a cruise line. I kept a dated ledger of every call. This talk is what it says, anonymized, the operating model it produced, and what didn’t survive contact. What they had: agents riding employees’ tokens at a regulated bank; an LLM proxy in place while apps behind it called providers with their own API keys; 2,000 personal agents in one low-code platform; 67,000 APIs in one gateway and no policy anyone could name. What converged across 14 calls on MCP alone: a registry of what’s admitted, an identity per agent, a gateway agents can’t route around. The governance artifact is code: one YAML persona per agent kind in Git (owner, tools, data classes, action contract), reviewed as a pull request, compiled on merge into the registry row and gateway policy. Promotion is a PR. What failed rides along: paper policy, header allowlists.

talks.title: Twelve Consoles, One Investigation
talks.abstract: Security teams do not lack tools they lack the connective layer between them. Answering a simple question like “is this login legitimate?” often requires hopping across a dozen siloed consoles, manually pasting context, and performing cross system correlation entirely in an analyst’s head. To eliminate this bottleneck, we paired an ex-law enforcement investigator with a security engineer to build an automated, agentic investigation system. By routing queries dynamically across enterprise integrations, the system exposes hidden, multi-system threats, such as a localized login hiding an impossibly high network latency, or a Latveria RF signature on a device reporting an American IP. Attendees will walk away with practical, production-tested blueprints: a GET-pinned read-only driver pattern, indicator-based routing logic, and a permission model designed for safe, unattended operation.

talks.title: Agentic AI in the Wild: What Real Deployments Teach Us About Governance and Scale
talks.abstract: Agentic AI is moving into production, but real deployments look nothing like conference demos. Drawing on research across 28 organizations, from 20-person startups to 20,000-employee companies, Chenxi Wang and Jasmine Jaksic examine how teams expand autonomy, measure success, and manage risk. We found that while many agent use cases are single-step or transactional, enterprises find the most value with long-horizon deployments. The strongest autonomous use cases today are bounded, high-volume, repeatable, auditable, and reversible. Jasmine complements that research with real agents built at NVIDIA, showing why successful demos fail in production. One looked strong until it was tested against representative work. Another reasoned coherently from incomplete enterprise state. A third exposed how a security control can deadlock the platform. Together, these experiences show that production readiness must be evaluated across the model, workflow, platform, and authority boundary.

talks.title: TBA
Integrous AI Systems Design

speakers.name: Bruce Schneier
speakers.affiliation: Fellow and Lecturer, Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Toronto

talks.abstract: In computer security, the CIA Triad represented the three security properties systems should have: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Of the three, integrity has been the most elusive; and, in an AI-powered internet-of-things world, the most important. This talk explores all the facets of integrity: data, processing, storage, and contextual. If we are ever going to trust these systems to take complex actions on our behalf – we are going to need to solve integrity.

talks.title: TBA
Giving AI Religion

speakers.name: Sounil Yu
speakers.affiliation: Creator of the Cyber Defense Matrix and the DIE Triad

talks.abstract: Least privilege is inadequate for agents. This shortfall has led to an alt. approach: “least agency.” When “least agency” is viewed through a one-dimensional Fate versus Free Will lens, responsibility and accountability diverge, suggesting that shared responsibility models may not work for agents. Instead, we may need a shared accountability model. This talk introduces the C4 model (Crown, Chassis, Conscience, Committee) to map out how and where we can control agents and who would be accountable at various control points. C4 is well aligned with other models for regulation making it theoretically grounded, but its application towards Agentic AI makes it experimentally interesting. Moreover, C4’s theological framing introduces an intriguing experiment: can a deliberately manufactured “miracle,” delivered through the Chassis, override an agent’s behavior contrary to its goals? We’ll show empirical test results demonstrating how engineered miracles can meaningfully compel AI obedience.

talks.title: We don’t need an LLM for That
talks.abstract: Zero-shot LLMs are easy to deploy, therefore stakeholders ask why fund classical ML. We test this assumption using zero-shot frontier LLMs, XGBoost, fine-tuning, and two LLM-ML ensembles, on phishing and network attack detection. Three network datasets come from one Mirai capture rebuilt at three aggregation levels, isolating representation as the variable. The answer is nuanced. On phishing, zero-shot LLMs hit 0.970 AUCPR, but a fine-tuned encoder beats them at 0.998. On network traffic, zero-shot LLMs are guessing “attack” almost every time, with one narrow exception that still trails XGBoost. XGBoost stays strong, and routing uncertain cases to the LLM makes results worse. A high class prior or a leaky split can each fake an “LLMs work” result, a trap fine-tuning or evaluation on network data hits. We bring fine-tuning runs, AUCPR-vs-class-prior numbers across four representations, and a decision guide: which model, which representation, per task and budget.

talks.title: Lunch break
Lunch break
Lunch break
Victim as a Service: Defending Against Trust Based Scams using AI
talks.abstract: Pig butchering and other interactive online scams build trust over weeks or months, making them highly effective and difficult to disrupt with traditional defenses. In this talk, I’ll describe how we built an LLM-driven system that defends against these scams at attacker scale. By safely sustaining realistic, long-term engagement with scammers, the system maintains thousands of convincing dialogues, and recognizes and responds to the milestones scammers use to move victims toward payment. I’ll conclude with how these AI-powered interactions reveal signals that can help defenders detect escalating scams earlier, increase friction for fraudsters, and intervene before victims lose money.

talks.title: Approval Is Not Human Presence: Building and Breaking an MCP Permission Broker

speakers.name: Brooks McMillin
speakers.affiliation: Security Engineer & AI Security Researcher, Dropbox

talks.abstract: An AI agent on a developer workstation often inherits the same UID, groups, environment, and credentials as its human operator. In that setting, an “Approve” action is just input the agent may be able to generate and not necessarily evidence that a human participated. This talk presents a deployed MCP permission broker that requires evidence of human presence before granting sensitive capabilities as well as allowing for different coding agent sessions running as the same user to have different permissions. I’ll reconstruct a live boundary test run from the strongest position the agent held: the human’s UID, membership in the admin group, a writable source checkout, and a valid broker session. Attendees will leave with a practical threat model, enforcement pattern, and adversarial test plan for making human approval a real security boundary.

talks.title: CTF
Fuzzing Native Node.js Dependencies with LLMs
talks.abstract: A hands-on workshop using LLMs to generate fuzzing harnesses and corpora for native Node.js dependencies, verify results, and automate the fuzzing process.
talks.details: Description: Building the fuzzing harness and the starting corpus has traditionally been one of the most time-consuming parts of fuzzing. In this workshop, we remove that bottleneck with LLMs. By letting an LLM read the code and generate the harness and corpus, we cut the time to first results and open the door to automating the whole fuzzing process. Prerequisites: Basic experience in using a coding model Basic understanding of fuzzing Familiarity with Node.js and basic C/C++ helps but is not required. Participant Setup Requirements: Participant should have a laptop that: has Docker (or a compatible OCI-compliant container runtime) is not blocked from running the afl++ program by EDR/XDR or similar.

talks.title: Specification – Driven Coding

speakers.name: Jordan Hubbard
speakers.affiliation: Sr. Director, NVIDIA. Speaker to code consultant

talks.abstract: Learn how a meta-harness captures prompts and agent actions while keeping code, documentation, specifications, and the development lifecycle aligned.
talks.details: Description: Vibe coding makes it easier than ever to build your first app—even one with surprisingly complex features. But keeping the work organized is another challenge: prompts and agent actions can go unrecorded, while code, documentation, specifications, and the development lifecycle fall out of sync. In this session, you’ll learn to use a meta-harness that brings it all together in one tool. It captures the work as you go and keeps your code structured, documented, and specified throughout development. Prerequisites: Must understand at least the essentials of software development, including one programming language, and the basics of building software using make, cmake, bazel, or similar build system. Must have Linux, macOS or Windows laptop Participant Setup Requirements: http://github.com/jordanhubbard/literate-ai and any development tools for their environment – xcode for macOS, visual studio for Windows, C compiler + python for Linux

talks.title: Benign Until It Isn’t: Build a Sleeper Skill, Then Catch It
talks.abstract: Workshop participants build and audit sleeper skills, then test layered detection, acceptance checks, and runtime guardrails for safe agent containment.
talks.details: Description: Your team is already installing agent skills, or is about to, and the review step most people rely on returns a verdict that does not mean what it sounds like. A skill can pass scanning and human review, then reach files, tools, and identity surfaces its description never mentions. Or it can behave one way under review and another way once it ships. This workshop teaches you to catch both by making you build them first. In a contained sandbox, you audit a skill that already carries a benign verdict and map what it can actually reach, dependency chain and identity-file writes included. Then you build a sleeper skill yourself, watch it pass the gate, and watch it wake up, so the detection signal is something you have seen rather than read about. The second half is defense. You run static, dependency-graph, and behavioral runtime detection across a mixed set of skills, score where each layer catches and misses, then write an acceptance checklist and runtime guardrails and test them against your own sleeper. The target is containment that does not lobotomize the agent. You leave with the checklist, the guardrails, and the sandbox. Prerequisites: Comfort reading code and configuration, mostly Python and JSON-style files, and basic command-line or browser-IDE use. No AI or machine-learning background is required and no prior experience with agent skills is assumed; the session defines what it needs as it goes. If you have ever reviewed a dependency or written a detection rule, you are over-qualified for the entry bar and will get plenty out of the later modules. Participant Setup Requirements: A laptop with a modern browser and nothing installed. Lab accounts are pre-issued on site, so there is no signup, no personal email login, and no admin rights needed. If you prefer to work locally instead of in the hosted sandbox, install Docker and clone the workshop repository beforehand; the repo link will arrive roughly one week ahead. Either path works and you can switch mid-session.

talks.title: AI Inference and its Privacy and Confidentiality Challenges
talks.abstract: Massive amounts of private data now flow daily into AI inference clusters, coming from individual users, startups, and large enterprises alike. Can providers actually uphold privacy and confidentiality to a meaningful bar? And can anyone operate such guarantees at scale today without unacceptable costs? We’ll review the challenges of building private inference infrastructure, the tradeoffs involved, and the common factor underlying every existing deployment, along with its real-world performance impact based on actual production systems. We’ll also cover a few new threats specific to confidential inference: attack surfaces that emerge not from classical infrastructure, but from the way LLMs themselves work and are operated. Expect a grounded look at what confidential inference can deliver today, where the sharp edges are, and what it takes to harden these systems against the many threats to privacy hiding in modern infrastructure.

talks.title: Reading the Residual Stream: Productizing Activation-Probe Security at Intuit

speakers.name: Guy Shtar
speakers.affiliation: AI Security & Safety Architect | GenAI Security, Threat Modeling, and AI-Assisted Risk Assessment, Intuit

speakers.name: Guy Elad
speakers.affiliation: AI Science Tech Lead, AI Security, Intuit

talks.abstract: Production guardrails come in two flavors: LLM judges — a full autoregressive pass per check, and a judge that can itself be prompt-injected — and trained text classifiers: cheap, but blind to paraphrase, obfuscation, and image-borne attacks. This talk makes the case for a third path: generation-free guardrails. One forward pass through a small (2–4B) open-weight model, read its internal activations, classify them with lightweight probes — no tokens generated, no prompt to inject into, and the signal is what the model understood, not what the text says. We show how to build one: which signals to read, training probes with modest labeled data, and the engineering that makes it production-grade — activation extraction with early exit, cross-request GPU batching (~4.1s to under 820ms, bit-exact), calibration at sub-0.1% FPR. We compare against open detectors and frontier judges on 20+ public datasets, and share what broke on the way to production at a large fintech.

talks.title: Agent Authorization Is Not a Vault Problem
talks.abstract: Almost every agent-approval product shows the human a summary produced by the thing being approved. The signature covers bytes, the human reads prose, and nothing binds the two. We built the device that has to see, display and approve the exact bytes before a key signs: a real USB authenticator that gates ssh logins and FIDO2 assertions on a physical button. Then we attacked our own protocol before implementing it. Our first design had the desktop signing bytes chosen by the remote server, which is a signing oracle wearing a co-authorization costume. Our bring-up firmware answered plaintext control frames on an unprivileged HID channel. The transferable finding: any co-authorization design that reaches for a detached signature over the operation has probably built the same oracle. All open source, MIT OR Apache-2.0.

talks.title: Engineering Context for SOC Agents: Lessons, Failures, and Open Questions

speakers.name: Dan Dye
speakers.affiliation: Cloud Security AI Engineer, Google Cloud Security

talks.abstract: I started building SOC AI workflows with a simple setup: Markdown AI runbooks (what we now call Agent Skills) piped into a local Cline harness, and it worked surprisingly well. Moving to an enterprise agent platform opened an embarrassment of riches, but created a whole new set of engineering dilemmas that I am still figuring out. I now have persistent investigation memory for free, but how do I pick which memories are relevant? I can ground SIEM telemetry with the entirety of enterprise context, but what context should I actually inject? Given Model Garden, how do I decide which model to use? This talk is not corporate shilling for Google’s agent platform; it is an honest inquiry from a software builder and architect in the trenches. I will share what I’ve tried, what broke, the problems I’ve seen and heard, the trade-offs I am wrestling with, and open questions. I would love to compare notes with the audience.

talks.title: Everyone Wants All the AI Tools. Good.
talks.abstract: At a fast-moving tech company, everyone wants every AI tool, by this afternoon. They should. These tools are incredibly powerful. The problem is that agents are designed to finish the task, not respect risk tolerance they were never given. This talk covers how to govern AI without defaulting to “no” or sending every use case through central review. Start by aligning leadership on risk and redlines. Turn that into self-service paved roads, secure agent sandboxes, technical guardrails, and detection or blocking for the paths outside your tolerance.

talks.title: Building Security Review Agents: the Models are the Reliable Part
talks.abstract: Employees connect third-party and custom apps to Google Workspace and Slack [and more] faster than a small security team can review them. This is not an AppSec review: there is no author to interview and no build to block, just a client ID and a list of permissions describing access someone is already using. We built a review pipeline where several models assess each grant independently, a stronger model referees when they disagree, and a human decides. We wrapped that non-deterministic core in deterministic guardrails, which is exactly what you are supposed to do. Then we audited it. The verdict we stored disagreed with the reasoning we showed the reviewer. A model quietly stopped counting toward the score. A service ran clean for twelve days and produced nothing. Almost nothing that went wrong was the model. This talk is what we found, what we fixed, and why a human is still in the loop.

Enterprise OpenClaw: Tackling Agentic Security at Scale
talks.abstract: Work inside a modern company rarely lives in one place, and while having an AI agent execute tasks across GitHub, Slack, and production systems sounds great, it is a security nightmare if not properly architected. This talk explores how Felix Pago built an identity-aware, secure agent runtime using OpenClaw to run AI workflows at scale. We will dive deep into the systems engineering required for secure AI tool use: separating Requester, Actor, and Persona via our explicit actAs model, eliminating long-lived credentials via ephemeral token minting, sandboxing with gVisor, and enforcing read-only guardrails. Move beyond prompt engineering and learn how to actually build and operate an audited, least-privilege agent fleet of over 500 pods in production.

talks.title: From Patch Generation to Evidence: Building Trust in AI-Generated Code
talks.abstract: AI can generate patches faster than humans can review them. The next challenge is deciding whether these patches deserve our trust. This talk shares the engineering lessons that shaped the OpenAnt Auto Patcher trust architecture: which forms of evidence proved useful, which intuitive ideas failed to improve quality, and how controlled experiments refined the boundary between LLM reasoning and deterministic policy. This session focuses on designing systems that make, and communicate, trustworthy decisions. Beyond sufficient regression tests, flow analysis, and other known techniques, using agents, we can build trust in the system and the patches generated. For example, are patches for past vulnerabilities, generated by Auto Patcher, semantically equivalent to patches previously generated by maintainers? Then, how do we train our system based on that? Attendees will leave with practical principles for designing autonomous patching systems and, by extension, AI-assisted systems.

talks.title: Same Threat, Two Verdicts: Shadow Testing Our SOC Agent
talks.abstract: Our autonomous SOC agent has handled 5,000 threats a day for a year, yet the same threat could yield two well-supported but opposite verdicts. When a metric moved, was it the change or instability? We split the end-to-end agent: an investigation agent writes structured findings; a verdict agent reads only them and decides. This did not eliminate nondeterminism but revealed whether instability came from evidence or judgment. A/A test runs traced most variation to our playbooks, flat lists of 10–15 questions; the agent picked a different subset each run. Recipes replaced them: staged plans of mandatory and optional steps naming the evidence to seek and the tool to use. With baseline variance measured and reduced, shadow tests became meaningful: a silent candidate runs on the same threats as production, scored on agreement, FPR and precision against analyst ground truth and expected noise. Attendees learn to decompose, constrain, measure, and safely ship changes to production agents.

talks.title: When Humans Can’t Make It Hard Enough: Self-Hardening Environments for Frontier AI Investigators
talks.abstract: Attacks are going out of distribution. Hiding tracks, tampering with logs, even AI-driven zero-days: in a real 2026 incident, AI agents faked their own tool calls and tried (and failed) to delete their logs. Our tests can’t keep up: hard cyber evals and public benchmarks like Splunk’s BOTS are saturating. Training a good investigator already works, once it can practice in realistic environments. For SOC investigation those barely exist, so the scarce thing is building them at scale. We call this env-play: a generator improving its scenarios against a fixed investigator, hunting the hardest still-solvable cases. Every scenario is judged on three dimensions: realism, solvability, and difficulty. We’ll show what broke GPT-5.6-Sol (right verdict in ~8% of runs), what didn’t (noise, scripted tricks), and why we read its queries, not its score, in a live demo. You’ll leave with a loop for testing whether your agent can investigate or has merely learned your benchmark.

talks.title: BITE – Behavior-Intent Traceable Evaluation
talks.abstract: Scanners for extensions, skills, and MCP servers hit a precision wall: too many false positives. We address this by mapping behavioral signals, connecting them into chains, and interpreting them against the program’s intent. The flow: 1. Map signals such as credential reads, outbound calls, and file writes. Each can be legitimate on its own. 2. Connect signals into behavior chains. 3. Apply BITE (Behavior-Intent Traceable Evaluation): compare each chain with stated intent to decide whether it is legitimate, risky, or malicious. BITE is the key innovation. Rather than use the model as a black-box classifier, We ground its judgment in evidence from the artifact: code, connected behaviors, internal structure, and declared purpose. This reduces false positives, cost, and inconsistent judgments while keeping verdicts traceable to evidence. Stricter intent checks may also create false negatives. Using malicious cases, we show what failed, what improved, and where the approach falls short.

talks.title: When Evaluation Runs Start Talking to Each Other
talks.abstract: Agents assigned separate evaluation tasks can discover one another through shared infrastructure or public internet services, exchange answers and techniques, and build on work that persists across runs. These interactions can turn supposedly independent attempts into a system with shared memory and pooled effort, changing what the scores measure. Drawing on our work building and evaluating cyber agents, we examine how supporting infrastructure can become an alternative path to success, undermining evaluation validity and enabling unauthorized actions. During reinforcement learning, rewarding these shortcuts can also reinforce behavior the training process was meant to avoid. We examine why isolating execution alone does not establish independence, and how to preserve realistic tools and connectivity while protecting grading integrity and enforcing authorization boundaries.

talks.title: Threat Model Impossible: 1 Agent. 30 Days. 687 Security Reviews. And a Refrigerator.
talks.abstract: We built an in-house threat model agent that completed 687 AI-assisted security reviews in 30 days, documented 3k+ risks in Jira, and routed remediation to system owners. Building the agent wasn’t the hardest part. It was getting reliable system and ownership data, then using deterministic automation to turn AI output into structured Jira risk tickets. The pipeline starts with a 50-question owner survey. Copilot Studio reasons over the system artifacts. Power Automate validates the output and assigns the work. Humans then validate the results and escalate higher-risk systems into deeper threat model reviews using code, data-flow diagrams, and architecture documents. I’ll show what we built, how we scaled it, what broke, and how the agent ended up threat modeling unexpected things like a refrigerator. I’ll close with our plan to embed reviews into application platforms so they kick off as soon as systems are onboarded.
